questions.stem: Which of the following defines ethical leadership?
questions.key: Leading in a manner consistent with the Army Ethic and Army Values, especially when it is inconvenient, costly, or unobserved
distractors: Doing what is right, legally and morally, even when it is difficult
Leadership as an exchange of performance for reward or correction
Leadership that raises followers' motivation beyond self-interest
questions.explanation: Slide 6 defines ethical leadership as leading consistently with the Army Ethic and Army Values, especially when it is inconvenient, costly or unobserved.
why: That is the definition of integrity.
That describes transactional leadership.
That describes transformational leadership.

questions.stem: It is doing what is right, legally and morally, even when it is difficult, and even when reporting the truth costs the unit or the leader personally.
questions.explanation: Slide 15 defines integrity as doing what is right, legally and morally, even when difficult and even when the truth is costly.
why: Ethical leadership is leading in a manner consistent with the Army Ethic and Values.
Mission legitimacy is why ethics matters: operations within ethical and legal bounds preserve moral authority.
Accountability is one cost of integrity failures: legal and administrative consequences.

questions.stem: Which list shows the six steps of the ethical decision-making process in order?
questions.key: Define the problem, know the rules, develop courses of action, evaluate each COA, decide and act, reflect
distractors: Know the rules, define the problem, develop courses of action, evaluate each COA, decide and act, reflect
Define the problem, develop courses of action, know the rules, evaluate each COA, decide and act, reflect
Define the problem, know the rules, develop courses of action, decide and act, evaluate each COA, reflect
questions.explanation: Slide 10 lists the process as 1 Define the Problem, 2 Know the Rules, 3 Develop Courses of Action, 4 Evaluate Each COA, 5 Decide and Act, 6 Reflect.
why: Know the rules comes second, after the dilemma is defined.
Courses of action are developed after the rules are known.
Each COA is evaluated before the leader decides and acts.

questions.stem: Before choosing a response to a false compliance report, a commander lists the laws, regulations, orders and Army Values at stake. Which step of the ethical decision-making process is this?
questions.explanation: Identifying the applicable laws, regulations, orders and Army Values at stake is step 2, Know the Rules.
why: Defining the problem identifies the dilemma and the values or duties in tension.
Developing courses of action generates feasible options.
Evaluating each COA tests options against legal, moral and practical considerations.

questions.stem: A leader tests a course of action by asking, "Is it lawful and within regulations and orders?" Which ethical lens is this?
questions.explanation: Slide 11: the rules-based lens asks whether the option is lawful and within regulations and orders (AFP Code of Ethics, Articles of War, SOPs).
why: Outcomes-based asks what result best accomplishes the mission and protects the force.
Virtue-based asks what a leader of strong character would do.
Management-by-exception is a transactional leadership component, not an ethical lens.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the three ethical lenses?
questions.explanation: Slide 11 gives three lenses: rules-based, outcomes-based and virtue-based. Management-by-exception is a transactional leadership component (slides 19-22), not an ethical lens.
why: Rules-based is one of the three lenses.
Outcomes-based is one of the three lenses.
Virtue-based is one of the three lenses.

questions.stem: It is the leadership model in which leadership is an exchange of performance for reward or correction.
questions.explanation: Transactional leadership is an exchange: performance for reward or correction, maintaining standards and discipline.
why: Transformational leadership is inspiration that raises motivation beyond self-interest.
Ethical leadership is leading in line with the Army Ethic and Values.
Management-by-exception (passive) is only one transactional behavior: intervening after problems occur.

questions.stem: Which list contains the Four I's of transformational leadership?
questions.key: Idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration
distractors: Idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, contingent reward
Idealized integrity, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration
Individualized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, idealized consideration
questions.explanation: Bass and Riggio's Four I's are idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation and individualized consideration.
why: Contingent reward is a transactional behavior.
The first I is idealized influence, not idealized integrity.
Influence goes with idealized and consideration goes with individualized, not the reverse.

questions.stem: A commander keeps COMSEC discipline personally even when no one is checking, so soldiers follow the example, not just the order. Which of the Four I's does this show?
questions.explanation: Idealized influence is leading by example as a role model soldiers want to follow, not just obey.
why: Inspirational motivation is communicating a compelling vision and purpose.
Intellectual stimulation is encouraging soldiers to question assumptions and innovate.
Individualized consideration is coaching and mentoring each soldier according to needs.

questions.stem: A platoon leader privately supports a soldier through a family crisis, adjusting duties while maintaining unit effectiveness. Which of the Four I's does this show?
questions.explanation: Individualized consideration is coaching and mentoring each soldier according to needs and potential, as in this unit-level example.
why: Idealized influence is acting as a role model.
Inspirational motivation is framing a compelling purpose.
Intellectual stimulation is inviting questions and innovation.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes Intellectual Stimulation?
questions.key: Encouraging soldiers to question assumptions and innovate on problems
distractors: Leading by example as a role model soldiers want to follow, not just obey
Communicating a compelling vision and sense of purpose behind the mission
Coaching and mentoring each soldier according to needs and potential
questions.explanation: Intellectual stimulation is encouraging soldiers to question assumptions and innovate on problems.
why: That describes idealized influence.
That describes inspirational motivation.
That describes individualized consideration.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of transactional leadership?
questions.explanation: Intellectual stimulation is one of the Four I's of transformational leadership. Transactional leadership has contingent reward and management-by-exception, active and passive.
why: Contingent reward is a transactional component.
Management-by-exception (active) is a transactional component.
Management-by-exception (passive) is a transactional component.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the augmentation effect found by Bass and Riggio?
questions.key: Transformational leadership does not replace transactional leadership; it augments it
distractors: Transformational leadership replaces transactional leadership once a unit matures
Transactional leadership is rarely needed when a unit has strong ethical leadership
Ethical leadership alone produces performance beyond expectations
questions.explanation: Slide 27 states transformational leadership augments transactional leadership, so units need both clear standards and shared purpose.
why: The research says it augments, not replaces.
Units still need the structure of clear standards from transactional leadership.
The slides do not claim ethical leadership alone produces this; the augmentation effect concerns transformational plus transactional.
